text: William Blake (28 November 1757 – 12 August 1827) was an English poet, painter, and printmaker who remained largely unrecognized during his lifetime but has since become a seminal figure in the history of Romantic-era poetry and visual art. His "prophetic works" were described by 20th-century critic Northrop Frye as forming "what is in proportion to its merits the least read body of poetry in the English language." Born on 28 November 1757 at 28 Broad Street (now Broadwick Street) in Soho, London, he was the third of seven children, two of whom died in infancy; his father, James, was a hosier who lived in London. William attended school only until age 10, after which he was educated at home by his mother, Catherine Blake (née Wright). Though the Blakes were English Dissenters, William was baptized on 11 December at St James's Church, Piccadilly, London. The Bible profoundly influenced him from an early age, and he recalled mystical experiences such as seeing God's face against his window, angels among haystacks, and being visited by the prophet Ezekiel. At age 10, he enrolled in drawing classes at Henry Pars's school in the Strand and began studying classical art through drawings of Greek antiquities purchased by his father, influenced by Raphael, Michelangelo, Maarten van Heemskerck, and Albrecht Dürer. On 4 August 1772, he was apprenticed to engraver James Basire for seven years at £52.10, becoming a professional engraver at age 21. Basire's line-engraving style was considered outdated, and Blake later crossed out Basire's name from a list of artistic adversaries. After two years, Blake copied images from Gothic churches in London, including Westminster Abbey, where he experienced visions of Christ with the Apostles and a procession of monks and priests, and heard their chants. He was briefly interrupted by schoolboys from Westminster School, one of whom he knocked off a scaffold, leading to the withdrawal of their access. In 1780, Blake became a student at the Royal Academy in Old Somerset House, where he rebelled against President Joshua Reynolds' emphasis on "general truth" and "general beauty," responding in marginalia with "To Generalize is to be an Idiot; To Particularize is the Alone Distinction of Merit." He also disliked Reynolds' apparent humility, which he viewed as hypocrisy. Blake became friends with John Flaxman, Thomas Stothard, and George Cumberland, who shared radical views, with Stothard and Cumberland joining the Society for Constitutional Information. In June 1780, Blake was reportedly in the front rank of a mob that attacked Newgate Prison during the Gordon Riots, a protest against a parliamentary bill revoking sanctions against Roman Catholicism. In 1781, Blake met Catherine Boucher, whom he loved after expressing his heartbreak and asking if she pitied him; he married her on 18 August 1782 in St Mary's Church, Battersea, with Catherine signing the contract with an X. The marriage was successful, and Catherine became his "partner in both life and work," assisting as an engraver and colourist, mixing and applying paint, including colouring the cover of Europe: A Prophecy. According to Alexander Gilchrist, the poet and wife did everything in making books except manufacturing paper, and they made the ink or colour. In 2019, Tate Britain's Blake exhibition highlighted Catherine's role. Around 1783, Blake published his first collection of poems, Poetical Sketches. In 1784, after his father's death, he and former apprentice James Parker opened a print shop and began working with radical publisher Joseph Johnson, whose house hosted intellectuals such as Joseph Priestley, Richard Price, John Henry Fuseli, Mary Wollstonecraft, and Thomas Paine. Blake supported the French and American revolutions, wore a Phrygian cap in solidarity, and composed the unfinished manuscript An Island in the Moon in 1784. He illustrated Original Stories from Real Life (1791) by Wollstonecraft, and in Visions of the Daughters of Albion (1793), condemned enforced chastity and marriage without love, defending women's right to self-fulfilment. From 1790 to 1800, Blake lived at 13 Hercules Buildings, Hercules Road, North Lambeth, London, a site now marked by a plaque and commemorated by 70 mosaics at Waterloo Station. In 1788, at age 31, Blake developed relief etching, which he used for most of his illuminated books, paintings, and poems. This method, also known as illuminated printing, involved writing text on copper plates with pens and brushes using an acid-resistant medium, then etching the plates to leave designs in relief. The resulting books were hand-coloured and stitched into volumes. Though relief etching is his most innovative technique, his commercial work primarily used intaglio engraving, a laborious process where images were incised into copper plates, taking months or years to complete. Europe Supported by Africa and America, an engraving for John Gabriel Stedman's The Narrative of a Five Years Expedition against the Revolted Negroes of Surinam (1796), depicts three women embracing, with Black Africa and White Europe holding hands in a gesture of equality, while the barren earth blooms beneath them; Europe wears pearls, and Africa and America wear slave bracelets. Some scholars interpret the bracelets as representing the historical reality of slavery, while the handclasp reflects Stedman's belief that people of different colors are created by the same hand. Blake used intaglio engraving for works such as the Illustrations of the Book of Job, completed just before his death. A 2009 study noted his use of "repoussage," a technique of hammering out mistakes by hitting the back of the plate, indicating the laborious nature of intaglio work. Blake and Catherine's marriage was close and devoted; he taught Catherine to write and she helped him colour his poems. Some biographers suggest he attempted to bring a concubine into the marriage according to Swedenborgian beliefs, though this is disputed. Samuel Foster Damon speculates that Catherine may have had a stillborn daughter for which The Book of Thel is an elegy. In 1800, Blake moved to a cottage in Felpham, West Sussex, to illustrate works by William Hayley, where he began Milton (title page dated 1804, completed in 1808). The preface to Milton includes a poem beginning "And did those feet in ancient time," which became the anthem "Jerusalem." Blake grew resentful of Hayley, believing he was preoccupied with "the meer drudgery of business," and wrote in Milton: A Poem, "Corporeal Friends are Spiritual Enemies." In August 1803, Blake was involved in a physical altercation with soldier John Schofield, who claimed Blake said "Damn the king. The soldiers are all slaves." Blake was cleared at the Chichester assizes, with the report noting the evidence was "invented" and thus led to acquittal. Schofield was later depicted wearing "mind forged manacles" in an illustration to Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion. In 1804, Blake returned to London and began working on Jerusalem (1804–20), his most ambitious work. After approaching dealer Robert Cromek to market an engraving based on Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, he was cheated when Cromek commissioned Thomas Stothard instead. Blake broke off contact with Stothard and held an independent exhibition in his brother's haberdashery shop at 27 Broad Street in Soho, showcasing his own version of the Canterbury illustration, titled The Canterbury Pilgrims. He wrote a Descriptive Catalogue (1809), which includes a "brilliant analysis" of Chaucer and is regularly anthologised as a classic of Chaucer criticism, along with detailed explanations of his other works. The exhibition was very successful.

Blake was later depicted wearing "mind forged manacles" in an illustration to Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion.[59] He returned to London in 1804 and began writing and illustrating Jerusalem (1804–20), his most ambitious work. Having conceived the idea of portraying characters from Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, Blake approached dealer Robert Cromek, intending to market an engraving; however, knowing Blake was too eccentric to produce a popular work, Cromek commissioned his friend Thomas Stothard to execute the concept. Upon learning he had been cheated, Blake severed contact with Stothard and held an independent exhibition in his brother's haberdashery shop at 27 Broad Street in Soho, designed to promote his own version of the Canterbury illustration (titled The Canterbury Pilgrims) along with other works. As a result, he wrote his Descriptive Catalogue (1809), which Anthony Blunt called a "brilliant analysis" of Chaucer and is regularly anthologised as a classic of Chaucer criticism; it also included detailed explanations of his other paintings. The exhibition was poorly attended, selling none of the temperas or watercolours, and its only review in The Examiner was hostile.[61] Around this time (circa 1808), Blake expressed strong views on art in a series of polemical annotations to Sir Joshua Reynolds' Discourses, denouncing the Royal Academy as a fraud and proclaiming, "To Generalize is to be an Idiot."[62] In 1818, he was introduced by George Cumberland's son to young artist John Linnell.[63] A blue plaque commemorates Blake and Linnell at Old Wyldes' in North End, Hampstead.[64] Through Linnell, Blake met Samuel Palmer, a member of the Shoreham Ancients, a group of artists who shared his rejection of modern trends and belief in a spiritual and artistic New Age. At age 65, Blake began work on illustrations for the Book of Job, later admired by John Ruskin, who compared Blake favourably to Rembrandt, and by Vaughan Williams, who based his ballet Job: A Masque for Dancing on a selection of the illustrations.[citation needed] In later life, Blake began selling a large number of his works, particularly his Bible illustrations, to Thomas Butts, a patron who viewed him more as a friend than as an artist of merit—this reflects the general opinion of Blake throughout his life.[citation needed] In 1826, a commission for Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy came to Blake through Linnell, with the aim of producing a series of engravings. Blake's death in 1827 cut short the project, and only a handful of watercolours were completed, with only seven engravings reaching proof form. Nevertheless, the Dante watercolours are among Blake's richest achievements, engaging fully with the complexity of the poem, and the mastery of watercolour reached a higher level, used to extraordinary effect in differentiating the atmosphere of the three states of being in the text. The illustrations are not merely accompanying works but appear to critically revise or comment on certain spiritual or moral aspects of the poem. Because the project was incomplete, Blake's original intent may be obscured; however, in the margin of Homer Bearing the Sword and His Companions, Blake notes, "Every thing in Dantes Comedia shews That for Tyrannical Purposes he has made This World the Foundation of All & the Goddess Nature & not the Holy Ghost," indicating his dissent from Dante's admiration of ancient Greece and his apparent glee in Hell's punishments. At the same time, Blake shared Dante's distrust of materialism and the corrupting nature of power and relished the opportunity to represent the atmosphere and imagery of Dante's work. Even near death, Blake's central preoccupation was his work on the illustrations for Dante's Inferno; he is said to have spent one of his last shillings on a pencil to continue sketching.[66] Blake's final years were spent at Fountain Court off the Strand (the property was demolished in the 1880s when the Savoy Hotel was built).[1] On the day of his death (12 August 1827), he worked relentlessly on the Dante series. Eventually, he ceased working and turned to his wife, who was in tears by his bedside. Beholding her, Blake is said to have cried, "Stay Kate! Keep just as you are – I will draw your portrait – for you have ever been an angel to me." Having completed this portrait (now lost), Blake laid down his tools and began to sing hymns and verses. At six that evening, after promising his wife he would be with her always, Blake died. Gilchrist reports that a female lodger present at his death said, "I have been at the death, not of a man, but of a blessed angel."[68] George Richmond described Blake's death in a letter to Samuel Palmer: "He died ... in a most glorious manner. He said He was going to that Country he had all His life wished to see & expressed Himself Happy, hoping for Salvation through Jesus Christ – Just before he died His Countenance became fair. His eyes Brighten'd and he burst out Singing of the things he saw in Heaven."[69] Catherine paid for Blake's funeral with money lent to her by Linnell. Blake's body was buried in a shared plot, five days after his death—on the eve of his 45th wedding anniversary—at the Dissenters' burial ground in Bunhill Fields, in the City of London area. His parents' bodies were also buried there. Present at the ceremonies were Catherine, Edward Calvert, George Richmond, Frederick Tatham, and John Linnell. After Blake's death, Catherine moved into Tatham's house as a housekeeper and believed she was regularly visited by Blake's spirit. She continued selling his illuminated works and paintings but entertained no business transaction without first "consulting Mr. Blake."[71] On her death in October 1831, she was calm and cheerful, calling out to him "as if he were only in the next room, to say she was coming to him, and it would not be long now."[72] Following her death, Frederick Tatham took possession of Blake's works and continued selling them. Tatham later joined the fundamentalist Irvingite church and, under conservative influence, burned manuscripts he deemed heretical; the exact number of destroyed works is unknown, but shortly before his death Blake told a friend he had written "twenty tragedies as long as Macbeth", none of which survive.[74] William Michael Rossetti also burned works by Blake he considered lacking in quality,[75] and John Linnell erased sexual imagery from a number of Blake's drawings.[76] At the same time, some unpublished works were preserved by friends, such as his notebook and An Island in the Moon. Blake's grave is commemorated by two stones. The first reads "Near by lie the remains of the poet-painter William Blake 1757–1827 and his wife Catherine Sophia 1762–1831" and is located approximately 20 metres (66 ft) from the actual grave, which was not marked until 12 August 2018.[44] Since 1965, the exact location of Blake's grave had been lost and forgotten due to damage from the Second World War; gravestones were removed and a garden created. The memorial stone, indicating the burial sites are "nearby," was listed as a Grade II listed structure in 2011.[77][78] A Portuguese couple, Carol and Luís Garrido, rediscovered the exact burial location after 14 years of investigation, and the Blake Society organised a permanent memorial slab, unveiled at a public ceremony on 12 August 2018.[44][78][79][80] The new stone is inscribed "Here lies William Blake 1757–1827 Poet Artist Prophet" above a verse from his poem Jerusalem. The Blake Prize for Religious Art was established in Australia in 1949. In 1957, a memorial to Blake and his wife was erected in Westminster Abbey.[81] Another memorial lies in St James's Church, Piccadilly, where he was baptised. At the time of his death, Blake had sold fewer than 30 copies of Songs of Innocence and of Experience.[82] Blake was not active in any well-established political party. His poetry consistently reflects a rebellion against the abuse of class power, as documented in David Erdman's Blake: Prophet Against Empire: A Poet's Interpretation of the History of His Own Times (1954). Blake was concerned about senseless wars and the blighting effects of the Industrial Revolution, and much of his poetry uses symbolic allegory to recount the effects of the French and American revolutions. Erdman claims Blake was disillusioned with the political outcomes, believing they had replaced monarchy with irresponsible mercantilism. Erdman also notes Blake was deeply opposed to slavery and that some of his poems, read primarily as championing "free love," had their anti-slavery implications underemphasised.[83] A more recent study, William Blake: Visionary Anarchist by Peter Marshall (1988), classifies Blake and his contemporary William Godwin as forerunners of modern anarchism.[84] The British Marxist historian E. P. Thompson's final work, Witness Against the Beast: William Blake and the Moral Law (1993), argues that Blake was inspired by dissident religious ideas rooted in the thinking of the most radical opponents of the monarchy during the English Civil War. Because Blake's later poetry contains a private mythology with complex symbolism, his late work has been less published than his earlier, more accessible work. The Vintage anthology of Blake edited by Patti Smith focuses heavily on the earlier work, as do many critical studies such as William Blake by D. G. Gillham. The earlier work is primarily rebellious and can be seen as a protest against dogmatic religion, especially in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, where the figure represented by the "Devil" is a hero rebelling against an imposter authoritarian deity. In later works, such as Milton and Jerusalem, Blake presents a distinctive vision of humanity redeemed by self-sacrifice and forgiveness, while retaining his earlier negative attitude toward the rigid and morbid authoritarianism of traditional religion. Not all readers agree on the continuity between Blake's earlier and later works. Psychoanalyst June Singer writes that Blake's late work shows a development of ideas first introduced in his earlier works, namely, the humanitarian goal of achieving personal wholeness of body and spirit. In the final section of her expanded edition of The Unholy Bible, she suggests the later works are the "Bible of Hell" promised in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell. Regarding Blake's final poem, Jerusalem, she writes: "The promise of the divine in man, made in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, is at last fulfilled."[86] John Middleton Murry notes a discontinuity between Marriage and the late works, in that while the early Blake focused on a "sheer negative opposition between Energy and Reason," the later Blake emphasized self-sacrifice and forgiveness as the path to interior wholeness. This renunciation of the sharper dualism of Marriage of Heaven and Hell is evident in the humanisation of the character of Urizen in the later works. Murry characterises the later Blake as having found "mutual understanding" and "mutual forgiveness."[87] Regarding conventional religion, Blake was a satirist and ironist, as illustrated and summarised in his poem Vala, or The Four Zoas, one of his uncompleted prophetic books begun in 1797. The demi-mythological and demi-religious main characters of the book are the Four Zoas (Urthona, Urizen, Luvah and Tharmas), created by the fall of Albion in Blake's mythology. The work consists of nine books, referred to as "nights," outlining the interactions of the Zoas, their fallen forms, and their Emanations. Blake intended the book to be a summation of his mythic universe. The Four Zoas represent four aspects of the Almighty God, and Vala is the first work to mention them. In particular, Blake's God/Man union is broken down into the bodily components of Urizen (head), Urthona (loins), Luvah (heart), and Tharmas (unity of the body), with paired Emanations being Ahania (wisdom, from the head), Enitharmon (what can't be attained in nature, from the loins), Vala (nature, from the heart), and Enion (earth mother, from the separation of unity).[88] As connected to Blake's understanding of the divine, the Zoas are the God the Father (Tharmas, sense), the Son of God (Luvah, love), the Holy Ghost (Urthona, imagination), and Satan who was originally of divine substance (Urizen, reason), with their Emanations representing Sexual Urges (Enion), Nature (Vala), Inspiration (Enitharmon), and Pleasure (Ahania).[90] Blake believed each person had a twofold identity, one half good and the other evil. In Vala, both the character Orc and The Eternal Man discuss their selves as divided. By the time he was working on his later works, including Vala, Blake felt he had overcome his inner battle but was concerned about losing his artistic abilities. These thoughts carried over into Vala as the character Los (imagination) is connected to the image of Christ, and he added a Christian element to his mythic world. In the revised version of Vala, Blake added Christian and Hebrew images and describes how Los experiences a vision of the Lamb of God that regenerates his spirit. In opposition to Christ is Urizen and the Synagogue of Satan, who later crucify Christ, from whom Deism is born.[91] Blake did not subscribe to the notion of a body distinct from the soul that must submit to the rule of the soul, but saw the body as an extension of the soul, derived from the "discernment" of the senses. Thus, the emphasis in orthodoxy on denying bodily urges is a dualistic error born of misapprehension of the relationship between body and soul. Elsewhere, he describes Satan as the "state of error," and as beyond salvation.[92] Blake opposed the sophistry of theological thought that excuses pain, admits evil, and apologises for injustice. He abhorred self-denial,[93] which he associated with religious repression and particularly sexual repression:[94] "Prudence is a rich ugly old maid courted by Incapacity. He who desires but acts not breeds pestilence." (7.4–5, E35) He saw the concept of "sin" as a trap to bind men's desires (the briars of Garden of Love) and believed that restraint in obedience to a moral code imposed from the outside was against the spirit of life: "Abstinence sows sand all over / The ruddy limbs & flaming hair / But Desire Gratified / Plants fruits & beauty there." (E474) He did not hold with the doctrine of God as Lord, an entity separate from and superior to mankind;[95] this is shown clearly in his words about Jesus Christ: "He is the only God ... and so am I, and so are you." A telling phrase in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell is "men forgot that All deities reside in the human breast." Blake had a complex relationship with Enlightenment philosophy. His championing of the imagination as the most important element of human existence ran contrary to Enlightenment ideals of rationalism and empiricism.[96] Due to his visionary religious beliefs, he opposed the Newtonian view of the universe. This mindset is reflected in an excerpt from Blake's Jerusalem: "I turn my eyes to the Schools & Universities of Europe / And there behold the Loom of Locke whose Woof rages dire / Washd by the Water-wheels of Newton. black the cloth / In heavy wreathes folds over every Nation; cruel Works / Of many Wheels I view, wheel without wheel, with cogs tyrannic / Moving by compulsion each other: not as those in Eden: which / Wheel within Wheel in freedom revolve in harmony & peace." (15.14–20, E159) Blake believed the paintings of Sir Joshua Reynolds, which depict the naturalistic fall of light upon objects, were products entirely of the "vegetative eye," and he saw Locke and Newton as "the true progenitors of Sir Joshua Reynolds' aesthetic."[100] The popular taste in England at the time for such paintings was satisfied with mezzotints, prints produced by a process that created an image from thousands of tiny dots upon the page. Blake saw an analogy between this and Newton's particle theory of light.[101] Accordingly, Blake never used the technique, opting instead to develop a method of engraving purely in fluid line, insisting that: "a Line or Lineament is not formed by Chance a Line is a Line in its Minutest Subdivision[s] Strait or Crooked It is Itself & Not Intermeasurable with or by any Thing Else Such is Job." (E784) It has been supposed that, despite his opposition to Enlightenment principles, Blake arrived at a linear aesthetic that was in many ways more similar to the Neoclassical engravings of John Flaxman than to the works of the Romantics, with whom he is often classified.[102] However, Blake's relationship with Flaxman seems to have grown more distant after Blake's return from Felpham, and there are surviving letters between Flaxman and Hayley wherein Flaxman speaks ill of Blake's theories of art.[103] Blake further criticised Flaxman's styles and theories of art in his responses to criticism made against his print of Chaucer's.

Blake's work involves prints made through a process that creates an image from thousands of tiny dots, a method he compared to Newton's particle theory of light, though he never used it, instead developing a technique of engraving in fluid line, asserting that a line is not formed by chance but is itself, in its minutest subdivision, straight or crooked, and not measurable by or against anything else, as stated in "Such is Job" (E784). Though often classified with the Romantics, Blake's aesthetic is more aligned with John Flaxman's Neoclassical engravings, but his relationship with Flaxman deteriorated after Blake's return from Felpham, with Flaxman criticizing Blake's artistic theories in letters to Hayley, and Blake responding to criticism of his print *Chaucer's Caunterbury Pilgrims* in 1810 by rejecting Flaxman's styles and theories. After his death, Blake has been claimed by various movements for his use of symbolism and allegory, particularly as a forerunner of the 19th-century "free love" movement, which began in the 1820s and viewed state-sanctioned marriage as "legal prostitution" and monopolistic, aligning more with early feminist thought, especially Mary Wollstonecraft's writings, which Blake admired. Blake criticized contemporary marriage laws and traditional Christian notions of chastity, advocating for a second wife during a strained marriage due to Catherine's inability to bear children, and his poetry, such as "Why should I be bound to thee, O my lovely Myrtle-tree?" and "Earth's Answer," suggests support for multiple sexual partners; in "London," he references "the Marriage-Hearse" under the "youthful Harlot's curse," and *Visions of the Daughters of Albion* is widely read as a tribute to free love, with Bromion and Oothoon bound only by law, not love. Blake opposed law and love, condemning the "frozen marriage-bed," and in *Visions*, wrote: "Till she who burns with youth, and knows no fixed lot, is bound / In spells of law to one she loathes? and must she drag the chain / Of life in weary lust?" (5.21–3, E49). Algernon Charles Swinburne highlighted Blake's praise of "sacred natural love" unbound by possessive jealousy, which Blake described as a "creeping skeleton," and Swinburne noted Blake's *Marriage of Heaven and Hell* condemned "pale religious letchery." Edward Carpenter (1844–1929) was influenced by Blake's mystical emphasis on energy free from external restrictions. Pierre Berger noted that Blake's early views celebrated authentic love over duty, and Irene Langridge observed that free love in Blake's creed was intended for the edification of the soul. Michael Davis (1977) argued that jealousy separates man from divine unity, condemning him to a frozen death. S. Foster Damon noted that for Blake, the main obstacles to free love were corrupt human nature and hypocritical communication, not just societal intolerance or male jealousy. Thomas Wright (1928) observed that marriage should afford joy but often fails to do so, as couples' awareness of being chained diminishes their joy, and Pierre Berger analyzed Blake's early mythological poems like *Ahania* as showing marriage laws as a result of human fallenness from pride and jealousy. Some scholars note Blake's views on free love were qualified and evolved, with late poems like *The Sick Rose* warning of predatory sexuality; Magnus Ankarsjö observed that in *Visions of the Daughters of Albion*, the heroine becomes more cautious as she gains awareness of sexuality's dark side, asking "Can this be love which drinks another as a sponge drinks water?" and that Blake, like Mary Wollstonecraft, developed more circumspect views late in life. Given Blake's sense of human fallenness, Ankarsjö argues Blake does not fully endorse sensual indulgence in defiance of law, as all love in the fallen world is enchained; he records Blake supporting a commune with shared partners, though David Worrall read *The Book of Thel* as rejecting the proposal to take concubines from the Swedenborgian church. Blake's later writings show renewed interest in Christianity, reinterpreting Christian morality to embrace sensual pleasure, though with less emphasis on sexual libertarianism and more on "self-denial" inspired by love rather than authoritarian compulsion. Berger, more than Swinburne, emphasizes a shift in sensibility from early to later Blake, believing the young Blake overemphasized following impulses, while the older Blake developed a better-formed ideal of true love involving self-sacrifice. Mystical sensuality remains in late poems, notably in Blake's denial of the virginity of Jesus's mother, while later works emphasize forgiveness, redemption, and emotional authenticity. Northrop Frye noted Blake's consistency, stating that his notes on Reynolds at fifty were "exactly similar" to those on Locke and Bacon when young, and that phrases and lines reappeared up to forty years later; consistency was a central principle, and self-contradiction was one of his most contemptuous critiques. Blake abhorred slavery and believed in racial and sexual equality, with poems expressing universal humanity: "As all men are alike (tho' infinitely various)," and in one poem, a black child narrates that white and black bodies are like shaded groves or clouds, existing until one learns "to bear the beams of love," stating: "When I from black and he from white cloud free, / And round the tent of God like lambs we joy: / I'll shade him from the heat till he can bear, / To lean in joy upon our fathers knee. / And then I'll stand and stroke his silver hair, / And be like him and he will then love me" (23–8, E9). Blake remained engaged with social and political issues, opposing institutional restrictions, including the Church, and in *Songs of Experience* (1794), distinguished between the Old Testament God, whom he rejected for his restrictions, and the New Testament God, whom he viewed positively. From a young age, Blake claimed to have seen visions: at age four, he saw God "put his head to the window," causing him to scream; at age eight or ten, he saw "a tree filled with angels, bright angelic wings bespangling every bough like stars," which he reported to his parents, escaping punishment due to his mother's intervention. His mother was especially supportive, and early drawings and poems adorned her chamber. He also saw angelic figures among haymakers. Blake claimed to experience visions throughout his life, often involving beautiful religious themes, and believed he was personally instructed by Archangels, who actively read and enjoyed his works. In a letter to William Hayley (6 May 1800), he wrote: "I know that our deceased friends are more really with us than when they were apparent to our mortal part. Thirteen years ago I lost a brother, and with his spirit I converse daily and hourly in the spirit, and see him in my remembrance, in the region of my imagination. I hear his advice, and even now write from his dictate." In a letter to John Flaxman (21 September 1800), he wrote: "[Felpham] is a sweet place for Study, because it is more spiritual than London. Heaven opens here on all sides her golden Gates; her windows are not obstructed by vapours; voices of Celestial inhabitants are more distinctly heard, & their forms more distinctly seen; & my Cottage is also a Shadow of their houses. My Wife & Sister are both well, courting Neptune for an embrace... I am more famed in Heaven for my works than I could well conceive. In my Brain are studies & Chambers filled with books & pictures of old, which I wrote & painted in ages of Eternity before my mortal life; & those works are the delight & Study of Archangels." In a letter to Thomas Butts (25 April 1803), he wrote: "Now I may say to you, what perhaps I should not dare to say to anyone else: That I can alone carry on my visionary studies in London unannoy'd, & that I may converse with my friends in Eternity, See Visions, Dream Dreams & prophecy & speak Parables unobserv'd & at liberty from the Doubts of other Mortals; perhaps Doubts proceeding from Kindness, but Doubts are always pernicious, Especially when we Doubt our Friends." In *A Vision of the Last Judgement*, he wrote: "Error is Created Truth is Eternal Error or Creation will be Burned Up & then & not till then Truth or Eternity will appear It is Burnt up the Moment Men cease to behold it I assert for My self that I do not behold the Outward Creation & that to me it is hindrance & not Action it is as the Dirt upon my feet No part of Me. What it will be Questiond When the Sun rises do you not see a round Disk of fire somewhat like a Guinea O no no I see an Innumerable company of the Heavenly host crying Holy Holy Holy is the Lord God Almighty I question not my Corporeal or Vegetative Eye any more than I would Question a Window concerning a Sight I look thro it & not with it." (E565–6) Despite seeing angels and God, Blake also claimed to have seen Satan on the staircase of his South Molton Street home in London. William Wordsworth commented, "There was no doubt that this poor man was mad, but there is something in the madness of this man which interests me more than the sanity of Lord Byron and Walter Scott." John William Cousins wrote that Blake was "a truly pious and loving soul, neglected and misunderstood by the world, but appreciated by an elect few," who "led a cheerful and contented life of poverty illumined by visions and celestial inspirations." The 1911 *Encyclopædia Britannica* entry questioned whether Blake was mad, noting he was under the influence of illusions with no outward facts to account for them, and that much of his writing lacks logical coherence. Blake's work was neglected for a generation after his death and nearly forgotten until Alexander Gilchrist began his biography in the 1860s, which transformed his reputation, especially through adoption by Pre-Raphaelites like Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Algernon Charles Swinburne. In the 20th century, scholars such as S. Foster Damon, Geoffrey Keynes, Northrop Frye, and David V. Erdman helped establish Blake's standing. Blake influenced figures like William Butler Yeats, who edited his works in 1893, and British surrealists such as Paul Nash and Graham Sutherland, drawing on Blake's non-mimetic, visionary approach. British classical composers set Blake's poems, beginning with Doyne Bell's 1876 setting of "Can I see another's woe," followed by notable settings by Benjamin Britten, Ralph Vaughan Williams, and John Tavener, who set "The Lamb" (1982) and "The Tyger." June Singer argued Blake's views on human nature anticipate Carl Jung's ideas, with Jung noting Blake compiled half-digested knowledge in fantasies, which are artistic rather than authentic unconscious representations. Diana Hume George claimed Blake is a precursor to Freud's ideas.
